Below n = 2 the batch is marginally dearer, which is the shape a hoist has and is harmless. No behaviour change: `settle_cohort` already wrapped the whole batch in one storage layer, so collapsing the per-target layers changes nothing a caller can observe; the 07 §10 core events now deposit once per batch, matching the one computation they describe |
| SQ-498 | **A block-denominated enactment delay cannot prove epoch boundaries were crossed, because the logical epoch clock is crank-driven.** SQ-234 sized the `entrenched` delay at four maximum-length epochs of blocks, which is four boundary *crossings* exactly while the clock is advancing — and `epoch.tick` is permissionless `ensure_signed`, never a timer. `pallet-referenda` schedules enactment at `now + min_enactment_period` regardless, so on a chain nobody ticks for the whole delay an entrenched decision can enact having opened **no** new Baseline market, i.e. with none of the priced second opinion 06 §2.4 exists to buy. Closing it needs an epoch index captured at approval and re-checked at dispatch; referenda exposes no on-confirm hook, so it takes a two-phase **arm/apply** surface: the referendum enacts an `arm` call that records `(target, armed_at_epoch)`, and a second permissionless `apply` refuses until `current_epoch >= armed_at + 4`. That adds storage, an authority-matrix row per armable call, and a dispatch that can fail and need re-attempt — a liveness surface — which is why SQ-234 shipped the sizing instead. | 06 §2.1, §2.4; 05 §3.1 | 2026-07-26 (Codex review of PR #178, P1) | **✅ resolved 2026-07-26 (batch X)** — **ruled: the arm/apply surface is refused**, and 06 §2.4 now carries the decision rather than a tracked gap. No code change. Three reasons, in order of weight. (i) *The delay cannot buy what a stalled chain cannot sell.* The four boundaries exist to open new Baseline markets; on a chain whose clock is not advancing those markets do not open, so the second opinion is unavailable under either design — arm/apply does not deliver it, it withholds the decision until someone restarts the clock, and once anyone does, `tick` is permissionless and the boundaries accrue anyway. The designs differ only on a chain that stays dead: enact-without-opinion versus never-enact. (ii) It pays for that with a permanent new liveness dependency on the one track designed to be hardest to move — an `apply` that must actually be called, on the critical path of *every* entrenched decision, trading a clock assumption reachable only on a halted chain for a keeper assumption on all of them. (iii) **The quantitative point the row missed:** the delay is four *maximum-length* epochs, so it yields exactly four crossings only at the 42 d ceiling — at the 21 d default it yields **eight**. Losing the fourth boundary needs a clock that has lost more than half its expected advancement across 168 days, which is the halt 05 §4.8's detector already answers, not a subtle shortfall |
| SQ-499 | **Three permissionless cranks each reserve ~389 KB of proof for a payout that fires once per epoch.** SQ-490 replaced the A13 collator-compensation weight with a real benchmark, and its declared PoV is the generator's **estimated** 389,037 B (the recorded proof was 17,874 B — the estimator charges each of the 120 payees' `ForeignAssets::Account` keys as an independent maximum-depth trie path and ignores their shared asset prefix). Declaring the estimate is the correct conservative call, because under-declaring PoV yields blocks that exceed their proof budget at execution while over-declaring only costs capacity — and a sparse benchmark trie under-represents production path depth, so `pov_mode = Measured` would be optimistic about exactly the wrong thing. But the cost is real and now quantified: `decide` sits at **19.0 %** of the 3,932,160 B normal-class budget and `settle_cohort(12)` at **23.9 %**, so roughly four cranks fill a block's proof budget, and the payout they are being charged for happens on one crossing per epoch. **The remedy already exists in the spec for a different call:** 15 §4.5 requires a payload-executing extrinsic to pre-charge its worst case and refund actuals via post-dispatch info. Applying the same pattern to `tick`, `decide` and `settle_cohort` — return `DispatchResultWithPostInfo` and refund `collator_compensation()` on every path that did not cross an epoch — recovers the capacity without under-declaring anything. Cost: three dispatchables change return type, and every early-return/error path in them has to carry the refund, so the refund must be derived in one place rather than repeated (a missed path silently overcharges, which is safe, while a wrongly-applied refund undercharges, which is not). | 15 §4.5; 13 §5; 08 §6.3 | 2026-07-26 (SQ-490 implementation) | **✅ resolved 2026-07-26 (batch X)** — implemented. The three cranks return `DispatchResultWithPostInfo` and refund `collator_compensation()` on every path that did not pay. The pre-charge is unchanged (13 §5's pinned ceilings read `get_dispatch_info()` and did not move); this is post-dispatch only. Each pre-charge now lives in exactly one place — `tick_weight`/`decide_weight`/`settle_cohort_weight`, used by both the `#[pallet::weight]` attribute and the body — because a second copy that drifts would under-refund, which is the unsafe direction. Early `?` exits *before* the payout decision keep `actual_weight: None` and so pay the full charge: that is the safe direction and is commented at each call site so a later reader does not \"fix\" it. Verified by three tests asserting the exact refund, its absence on a crossing, and its presence on an error path |
| SQ-500 | **The guardian's per-block maintenance hook settles an unbounded-by-design 128-review sweep against a weight declaring roughly one-sixth of it, and the fixture that should have caught this excludes its own worst case.** `run_maintenance` (`pallets/guardian/src/lib.rs:1755`) collects every review matching `!ratified && !recall_scheduled && epoch > deadline_epoch` and settles each one in its own storage layer: `restore_due_review_fronting` (`ReviewFrontingOf`, `ReviewReferenda`, `VetoReviewReferenda`) then `settle_failed_review` (`ReviewFrontingOf`, `VetoReviewReferenda`, `FailedActions`, `Members`, `PendingBondReleases`, plus up to `GUARDIAN_THRESHOLD` bond slashes) plus a `load`/`persist` pair and its events — **at least 10 storage reads per overdue review**, and `reviews` is bounded at `MAX_REVIEWS = 128`. The saturated case is not hypothetical and not rare: `deadline_epoch = current_epoch + review_deadline_epochs` (`crates/guardian-core/src/lib.rs:798`), so **every review created in one epoch shares one deadline** and all of them fall due in the same block. A council that proposes and approves 128 actions inside one epoch therefore chooses which block carries a >= 1,280-read hook — and a captured council is precisely doc 14's threat model, so this is adversarially reachable, not merely a tail. The fix is runtime-code rule 3: bound the settles per block with defined overload behaviour (cursor + remainder to the next block, the idiom the epoch and oracle cranks already use), which also bounds the `iter_keys` scan, then benchmark the bounded batch at its worst case and drop the `tools/ci/generated-weight-overrides.toml` entry. The batch **rotates** behind a `MaintenanceSweepCursor`: settling is what drops a review out of the overdue filter, so a fixed `take(10)` would re-select one prefix forever and a batch-wide prefix of reviews that cannot settle (a stuck deposit refund) would suppress every review behind them permanently — a skip wearing the shape of a carry (Codex P2, correct). **The measurement corrected my framing twice.** First: "weight-neutral" was true of three dimensions and false of the fourth. | SQ-504 | **The execution guard's own fail-static migration halts cannot stick — the runtime erases them from a bitmap they never wrote, one statement later.** `pallet-execution-guard` latches `MigrationHalt::<T>::put(true)` directly at two production sites: `lib.rs:931`, whose own comment says "Keep retrying under an execution halt until operators repair the pin state" when the recovery-image pin is corrupt or missing, and `lib.rs:1656` in `migration_completed()`, when `release_recovery_image()` fails to unpin. The runtime, meanwhile, owns a source bitmap: `set_migration_halt_source` ORs a bit into `MigrationHaltSources` and `clear_migration_halt_sources` clears bits, and **both** end in `sync_execution_migration_halt(sources)`, which does an unconditional `MigrationHalt::put(sources & EXECUTION_HALT_SOURCES != 0)` (`runtime/bleavit-runtime/src/configs.rs:839-841`). The guard's direct writes never set a bit, so the bitmap reads 0 for them and any subsequent sync rewrites the flag to **false**. **In one case the erasure is immediate and unconditional.** The runtime's `MigrationStatusHandler::completed()` is literally `MigrationFailedStep::kill(); ExecutionGuard::migration_completed(); clear_migration_halt_sources(MIGRATION_FAILURE_HALT \| MIGRATION_STALL_HALT);` — so the halt set inside `migration_completed()` is cleared by the next statement of the same function whenever no `APPLIED_DETECTION_HALT` bit happens to be set, which is the ordinary completion path. The latch is not weak, it is inert. The same shape reaches `:931` through the recovery-reset and valid-applied clears. **Consequence is the status-quo-violating direction (R-7, G-1):** execution resumes while the condition the latch exists to hold is unrepaired, and the 09 §3.2(4) `MigrationHalted` diagnostic is never emitted for either site because that too hangs off the first-activation edge of the bitmap. **No test covers it, and the existing one encodes the bug**: `pallets/execution-guard/src/tests.rs:2113-2114` calls `GuardPallet::migration_completed()` and then `MigrationHalt::<Test>::put(false)` on the very next line, mirroring production rather than asserting survival. **Fix, and it subsumes a second open item:** give the guard's fail-static latches a source bit of their own, signalled through a `Config` seam, so they participate in the bitmap instead of racing it — which simultaneously makes them visible to the `MigrationHaltSources` activation-edge recorder that A14's `Π` instrumentation needs (the two `MigrationHalt::put(true)` sites are the highest-value entries on `Π`'s uninstrumented list for exactly this reason). The weaker alternative — OR semantics in `sync_execution_migration_halt` plus an explicit guard-side clear — leaves the diagnostic gap open. Genesis site `:1233` is out of scope: a genesis-staged halt is a spec'd drill affordance, though it inherits the same erasure and should adopt whichever mechanism lands. | 09 §3.2(4); 06; 15 I-10; R-7 | 2026-07-27 (batch X) | **open** — found while verifying A14's claim that the two sites "bypass `MigrationHaltSources`". Every step verified against HEAD (`configs.rs` 839-841 / 985-993, `lib.rs` 931 / 1655-1657, `tests.rs` 2113). Blocked on the A14 queue — `configs.rs` is touched by all four open PRs. |

A component admitted at `(3, 250)` — coverage 1,750 bps — keeps settling money at `(2, 150)`, coverage 450 bps, which may be far below its declared `Δs_max`. §6.3's whole purpose is that a lie costs more than it can move; after such an amendment it silently does not, with no event, no gate and no try-state signal. 07 §6.1 names the hazard for open games ("would let a lawful amendment retroactively under-collateralize a component that was admitted under the §6.3 coverage rule") and solves only that half. Two candidate closures: a constitution-side screening obligation on the two keys (reject an amendment that would break coverage for any live admitted component), or a re-check at snapshot time that flags/neutralizes the component instead. The first is fail-closed at the governance boundary and cheaper; the second is more permissive but needs a defined disposition for the newly-uncovered component. Adjacent to SQ-303. | 07 §6.3; §6.1; 13 §1 (`orc.bond_bps`, `orc.rounds`) | 2026-07-25 (SQ-341 scoping) | **resolved 2026-07-25** — closed at the **governance boundary**, the fail-closed half of the two options the row named: an amendment to either coverage input is refused (`CoverageBreaksAdmission`) if the resulting rate would fall below the `Δs_max` of any already-admitted attested component. Screening there rather than at snapshot time avoids ever having to define a disposition for a component that has become under-covered mid-life — it would have to either neutralize a component whose data is fine or let it settle uncovered. Built on the existing `BudgetDerivationGuard` seam (`CoverageGuard`, `()` permits, runtime binds), with the key set single-homed in `constitution-core::is_coverage_input` and the rate derivation still single-homed in `oracle_core::coverage_bps`. **Scope is every *registered* version, not only the frozen ones:** a version registered today activates later, and its components were admitted against today's ladder, so screening only the frozen set would let an amendment land in the window before activation and bite exactly when the component starts settling money. Directional — raising coverage is always legal, and with nothing admitted the screen stands aside entirely. **Two defects the implementation itself produced, both caught by its own tests.** (i) The first cut compared the proposed `orc.bond_bps` raw — it is a `Perbill`, parts per **billion**, against a `Δs_max` in **basis points** — so every proposed rate read ~100,000× more generous than it is and the screen waved through precisely the amendment it exists to refuse. This is SQ-212's trap recurring; the conversion now rounds **up**, matching `perbill_bps_param_or`, so rounding never overstates coverage. (ii) The `set_param` benchmark used a synthetic `bench.param` key, which short-circuits the screen — so the first regeneration reported *no* regression while measuring a call that never does the work (the SQ-489 shape, third occurrence). With a real coverage key and a saturated MetricSpec set the measurement is **3 → 21 reads**; acknowledged, and the benchmark now charges every `set_param` the worst case. Mutation-checked. |

Two questions: must `queue_time_check` be a superset of the guard's `enqueue` preconditions (making `decide` total), and is a nested `system.authorize_upgrade` intended to be admissible at all — 09 §2.1 describes a multi-item upgrade payload, which the top-level-only matcher cannot express? Fix: a shared domain-admission helper that re-derives every call, requires `domain_allowed(class, domain)` and rejects `InternalRootApplyUpgrade`, called from `static_check`/`queue_time_check` and reused in the epoch→guard enqueue adapter — making `decide` total. **Implemented:** `rederive_call` on `utility.batch_all([system.authorize_upgrade(h)])` yields `InternalRootApplyUpgrade` (the classifier matches `authorize_upgrade` only at top level), which `enqueue` refuses — while `static_check` returned `Eligible`, pinned by a test that failed pre-fix with exactly that. Fixed with the ruled shared helper `domains_admissible` in `configs.rs`, applied in `static_check` (T4 `SlashAll(ConstitutionViolation)`, matching the adjacent capability-failure disposition) and re-applied in the epoch→guard enqueue adapter, making `decide` total. The canonical top-level upgrade payload stays eligible, pinned by a positive test so the mirror cannot over-reject. **Review round corrected the disposition:** the first cut returned `SlashAll(ConstitutionViolation)` by analogy with the adjacent capability failure. 05 §2.1's T4 taxonomy governs and says otherwise — "confiscation requires a verified culpable act", and "the refund arm is the default and the two slash arms are the enumerated exceptions". This failure is in neither exception (footprint matches, capability passes, call re-derives cleanly); the only fault is a classifier projection artifact on `utility.batch_all`, a wrapper 05 §1.4 explicitly blesses. Now `Refund(ProcessHold)`. Taxonomy gap raised as SQ-362; the §1.1 enumeration gap as SQ-363. A later review round found that the false-footprint slash sat *after* the domain refund, letting a false declaration escape the T4 slash by co-occurring with a domain fault — fixed under SQ-480. |

| SQ-318 | **When does a T10-rejected proposal release its resource-domain locks?** 05 §1.4 says locks "are released **only at terminal transitions**", while 05 §2.1's *Terminal states* paragraph classifies `Rejected` with a healthy (non-`Voided`) vault as **transient** — terminal only at `Settled`, ~3 epochs later via T21 measurement. Holding the domain through the ~3-epoch measurement window that §2.1 makes this state transient for therefore protects nothing while blocking every other proposal touching the same domain, which §1.4's own collision paragraph already names as the pure **liveness cost** the design avoids where it buys no safety. Ruled **"released once no dispatch is reachable"**: T10 now releases the locks in both arms. The wave-1 change was right; what it lacked was the ruling and the evidence, both of which are now recorded. The Phase-0 simulation models no resource-lock contention at all, so no calibration evidence is invalidated. |

| SQ-380 | **The 07 §8 reserve probe is inert in production and its health flag is a one-way latch (critical; blocks SQ-205).** Two independent gaps compose into a trap. (a) `RuntimeProbeDispatch = ()` outside `runtime-benchmarks` (`runtime/bleavit-runtime/src/configs.rs`), so `ProbeDispatch::live()` is false and **no probe is ever sent**. (b) `XcmConfig::ResponseHandler = PolkadotXcm` (`runtime/bleavit-runtime/src/configs.rs:754`) rather than `bleavit_xcm::probe::ProbeAwareResponseHandler`, and no production type implements `bleavit_xcm::probe::ProbeSink` (the only impl is `runtime/bleavit-xcm/src/mock.rs:341`), so **`pallet_oracle::Pallet::reserve_probe_result` has zero production callers** and no probe *pass* can ever be recorded. But `crank_reserve_probe` commits `pending_since` regardless of `live()`, so its timeout folds still count fails: any signed keeper drives `ReserveUnhealthy` in ~`res.fail_threshold` probe intervals, and `res.recover_threshold` consecutive passes — the only exit — are unreachable. Today this is latent because the flag reaches nothing but `welfare_current().reserve_flag`; it becomes a chain-killer the moment SQ-205's sink is bound, since 08 §1.2 zeroes `spendable_nav` while the flag is set. Fix is B4's unfinished production binding: wire the response handler + a real `ProbeSink`, and bind `ProbeDispatch` to `XcmProbeDispatcher` (both impls already exist in `runtime/bleavit-xcm`), with the live-XCM admissibility re-verified as V-6 did. **A cheaper partial fix exists and was deliberately not taken**: gating `crank_reserve_probe`'s state advance on `T::ProbeDispatch::live()` would turn the latch into a no-op and make SQ-205's sink safe to bind live *today*, in files this branch already edits — the SQ-205 compliance review argued for exactly that. It was declined because it decides **SQ-385** (whether a structurally-absent probe scores as a fail per 07 §8's literal text, or advances no state at all) by implementation rather than by ruling, and either reading changes observable behaviour on a solvency path (R-1, R-7). Resolve SQ-385 first; if reading (b) wins, the `live()` gate plus binding the sink closes SQ-205 immediately. | 07 §8; 09 §6.1; 08 §1.2 | 2026-07-21 (SQ-205 implementation) | **resolved 2026-07-24 (stale — verified against HEAD)** — every claim is false at HEAD: `configs.rs` binds `RuntimeProbeDispatch = XcmProbeDispatcher<…>` in production, `XcmConfig::ResponseHandler = ProbeAwareResponseHandler<PolkadotXcm, RuntimeOracleProbeSink>`, and that sink calls `Oracle::reserve_probe_result`, so probe passes are reachable and the latch has an exit. The `ReserveProbeArmed` design added to 07 §8 also removes the pre-arm fail accrual the row described. Live Asset Hub calibration remains separately tracked by the release manifest's `treasury.reserve_probe_unverified` blocker, which is ops evidence, not a code gap. |

| SQ-385 | **What is the reserve-health metric `R` on a chain where no probe can be sent or answered?** 07 §8's scoring says "no probe sent (keeper outage) ⇒ probe **fail**. Absence is never healthy", while §8(3) makes recovery depend on `res.recover_threshold` consecutive **passes**. Neither contemplates SQ-380's situation, where the dispatcher and the response router are absent *by construction*, so fails accrue and passes are unreachable — the scoring rule and the recovery guarantee contradict each other. | SQ-182 | **No A8-owned crank connects the oracle money deadline to neutralization.** The oracle pallet exposes `force_neutralize_expired`, but the epoch/reporting integration has no bounded path that guarantees the no-report component is neutral-settled by the money deadline before cohort settlement. Assign the keeper/tick trigger and prove the deadline ordering. | 07 §11; 05 §6 | 2026-07-17 (B1b compliance review) | **resolved 2026-07-25 — and the row's own "assign the trigger" framing understated it twice.** The oracle side was finished and uncalled, so the money deadline was unenforced end to end; the missing piece was the **seam**, and `pallets/epoch::OracleAccess` now carries `note_settle_deadline(m)` and `note_epoch_boundary(ended)` alongside `any_open_dispute_touching`, both **undefaulted** so a runtime cannot leave either unbound invisibly. A new `drive_oracle_boundaries(index, phase)` runs from all three clock-syncing entry points (`tick`, `decide`, `settle_cohort`), driving a bounded, resumable `OracleDeadlineCursor` — `OracleSettleDeadline(m) = start of epoch(m+1) Housekeeping`, so Housekeeping of `N` makes every `m <= N-1` due and earlier phases only `m <= N-2`. **The ordering the row asked me to prove is not the one it names.** `settle_cohort` never reads `ComponentValues`; it reads the welfare *snapshot*. The consumer is `pallet-welfare::record_snapshot(m)`, which fails `MissingComponent` while a contested component has none, so the real chain in Housekeeping of `N` is `note_settle_deadline(N-1)` → `record_snapshot(N-1)` → `settle_cohort(N-3)`, each fail-closed against the one before. An adversarial review caught my first inline justification stating the wrong consumer; the comment and 07 §11(1) now state the true chain. `settle_cohort` additionally drives its **own** cohort's due measurement epochs, which is what makes the guarantee hold by construction instead of resting on the catch-up budget. **A12's "d20 retained rounds" does cover the bond-only late-verdict half** — `force_neutralize_expired` retains the `Rounds` entry and marks it `money_settled`, per §11(1) — but the doc comment above it still claimed a later verdict "finds no round", a leftover from before retention landed; corrected. **Design notes.** The cursor deliberately defaults to 0 rather than being migrated abreast of the clock: a cursor that starts at the current index claims coverage it never provided, and the per-cohort leg trusts it to decide whether a mid-flight cohort's earlier epochs still need driving — an upgraded chain replays from 0 at bounded no-op cost instead. The catch-up bound is `MAX_NON_TERMINAL_COHORTS`, **derived not picked**: a round can exist only for a measurement epoch some live cohort consumes (`report` requires `is_expected_spec_version`), so that is exactly the number of epochs that can carry non-trivial work; rowed in 13 §2 with a limit-coverage classification and marked test. **One live defect fixed in passing, surfaced by the review:** `expected_components` returned every component of the spec, so the newly-live deadline crank would have written neutral **flagged** `ComponentValues` rows for class-1/2/3 on-chain components — the declared input to §10's two-consecutive-flag renormalization, and for gate inputs its VOID escalation. Filtered to `SourceClass::Attested`, the predicate `onchain_components` 200 lines above already used. try-state gained a phase-aware ceiling on both cursors (a first pass admitted `cursor == index` in any phase, i.e. `m = N-1` neutralized before its deadline). Five mutations each fail exactly one new test. **Restructured after the Codex review (3 P1, all valid).** The driver is now a permissionless crank of its own, `epoch.drive_oracle_boundaries` at call index 17, removed from `tick`/`decide`/`settle_cohort` — the review showed the epoch benchmarks never prime oracle storage, so the generated weight recorded **one** `Oracle::Rounds` read against a 128-entry bound, and priming it honestly is arithmetically impossible inline: 13 §5 pins `decide` at 231,055 B of proof under a 384 KiB ceiling while the oracle aggregate alone measures 356,514 B. Nothing was lost, because the ordering never rested on intra-dispatch sequencing — `record_snapshot` fails closed on `MissingComponent` — and 07 §11(1) calls this a *crank* while §13 gives the oracle no hooks, so a crank is the shape the spec asked for. It is benchmarked with the oracle aggregate primed to bounds, wired into the SafetyFilter matrix as a Public leaf, and planned by the keeper. The review's other P1 here was **the cursor is not evidence for a cohort**: a cohort forming after one of its measurement deadlines was driven had no `CohortSchedule` when `expected_components` resolved, so that drive covered none of its components — my `measurement >= cursor` guard then skipped exactly the epochs that needed re-driving, wedging `record_snapshot` permanently. The guard is gone; the crank re-drives every live cohort's due epochs unconditionally. |

| SQ-187 | **Shared Baseline semantics across late rerun windows are incomplete.** Pin which frozen window a rerun uses when its original epoch's shared Baseline has later proposal windows or an already-sealed boundary. | 04 §8.4; 05 §5.3; 06 §5.3 | 2026-07-17 (B1b R1 dual review) | **resolved 2026-07-20 (B1 tail; verified against `pallet-market`, then documented).** Shipped behaviour is fully determined — the spec simply never described the mechanism. The shared Baseline book stores **one window per distinct boundary triple** (`DecisionWindows: MarketId → BoundedVec<TwapWindow, 8>`) with **per-proposal ownership layered on top** (`DecisionWindowOwners: MarketId → BoundedVec<(ProposalId, start, trailing_start, end)>`), so sharing is by *identity of boundaries*, not by epoch: coinciding epoch-e proposals share one window and hold separate owner rows. Answering the row directly: a rerun **registers its own new window** from the fresh `decide_at` (`force_rerun_markets` recomputes `start`/`trailing_start` and calls `register_decision_window(baseline, pid, …)`), never reusing or mutating its pre-rerun window; an **already-sealed** earlier window is *not* an obstacle — it stays a distinct entry, and `consume_decision_windows` consumes **every** window a proposal owns at once ("including an earlier sealed extension attempt"), requiring all of them to be sealed first; and a rerun **cannot** read another proposal's boundaries, because every match is on the exact triple the reader owns. Eviction is reference-counted — a window and its checkpoints drop only once the *last* Baseline-sharing owner has consumed them. The capacity edge is handled, not open: the 8-distinct-boundary ceiling (13 §4 `TwapCheckpoints`) is checked **before any mutation** and fails closed with a regression test (`ninth_twap_checkpoint_boundary_is_rejected_without_mutating_full_ring`), and `shift_decision_window` shifts a dead-man deadline **in place** precisely to avoid a transient ninth boundary on a shared Baseline. Spec trued: 04 §8.4 gained a normative five-point paragraph pinning all of it. No code change. |
| SQ-188 | **The `delta + 1pp` force-rerun rule lacks a unique producer/binding.** Confirm whether guardian force-rerun sets the same durable rerun flag as T13 and which decision window consumes the increment. | 05 §5.4; 06 §5.3 | 2026-07-17 (B1b R1 dual review) | **resolved 2026-07-20 (B1 tail; verified against `epoch-core`, then documented).** Both halves answered, and the answer is that the code was already correct and unique — only the spec was silent. **Producer:** both rerun kinds set the *same* durable `Proposal.rerun` flag. T13 rerun-open sets it (`crates/epoch-core/src/lib.rs:1171`) and the guardian `force_rerun` sets it too (`:1141`) — notable because force-rerun goes `Trading`/`Extended`/`Queued → Extended` **directly**, never passing through the `Rerun` state, so it would have been easy for it to be a second unflagged regime. It is not. **Uniqueness** is enforced on the producer side: `force_rerun` is admissible only while `!p.rerun && !p.delayed_once` (`:1136-1137`), which is the code form of 06 §5.3's "at most one guardian rerun of either kind per proposal, ever". **Consumer:** `decide_engine` reads the flag once (`:1786`) and applies `+ ONE_PP` to the class δ (`:1861`), so there is exactly one consuming site. **Which window:** the rerun's own Extended window and only that one — each producer sets `decide_at := now + DECISION_EXTENSION` and `extended := true` in the same transition, so one `decide()` runs under the raised hurdle and step 6 (`!p.extended`) forbids a further extension; the hurdle can neither leak into a later window nor be inherited by a non-rerun proposal. Spec trued: 05 §5.4 gained a normative paragraph pinning the one-flag/one-window binding, and 06 §5.3's "covers both rerun kinds" sentence now says explicitly that this includes the δ+1 pp regime. No code change. |

| SQ-141 | **Measurement context is many-version while registry asks for one version, and several economic inputs lack owners.** Concurrent cohorts may freeze multiple MetricSpec versions for one measurement epoch, but `registry::EpochContext::frozen_spec_version` returns one `u16`; no bounded epoch-indexed source retains historical epoch-end timing; additionally no runtime storage presently owns `StakeAtRisk(c,m)` cohort escrow, registry milestone targets, welfare normalized on-chain/relay daily counters, or the certified `InCapPrize` envelopes for PARAM/CODE/META. Should the registry key become versioned and which pallets own these bounded inputs/timing? | 05 §4–§6; 07 §2/§6; 08 §5.2 | 2026-07-16 (B1a A8/A11 wiring) | **resolved 2026-07-25 (contract v14)** — ruled 2026-07-21 (batch X), code landed 2026-07-25; owner **A12**. Verified: the historical-timing claim is **stale** (B1b added a bounded, tested timing archive); the single-version registry premise is real and fails closed. 07 still keys `Aggregates` by epoch alone while §2 requires per-version games, so code could not pick a representation without a ruling. **Ruled: version the complete registry lifecycle by `(epoch, spec_version)`** — under G-1 it cannot silently combine claims governed by different frozen targets or formulas. **Scoped 2026-07-25 — the implementation's biggest risk is not the key change but what it makes reachable.** `incident_multiplier`'s miss-arm returns `FixedU64(1e9)` — "no incidents", the *favourable* value, as 07 §7 itself flags. That arm is near-unreachable today because `frozen_spec_version` returns `None` for any epoch with more than one live version, so a filing is either matched or refused. Once `Aggregates` is keyed by `(epoch, spec_version)`, a reader that asks for the wrong version — or asks before that version's `close_epoch` has run — silently gets full-strength `C_attested` for a cohort whose incidents were filed under the sibling version: a G-1 violation reached purely by a key change, with no error, no event and no try-state signal. The re-keying therefore needs a **fail-closed reader**, not a version-blind `get`. Two further notes: the re-key flips `file` from fail-closed to admissible at activation boundaries (intended, but it is a closed→open transition worth pinning), and 07 §7's storage table still reads "≤ 4 keys live", which the ruling contradicts and which must be amended to 4 × ≤2 versions. Registry **events** are the only 02-frozen part of the blast radius (`(epoch, filing_id)` stops being unique); making `FilingId` unique per *instance* would avoid touching them entirely. The ruling also assigns the orphaned inputs: epoch → timing; a snapshot owner over epoch/ledger state → `StakeAtRisk`; `MetricSpec` → milestone targets; the welfare/treasury producers → daily counters and certified capability envelopes. **Resolved 2026-07-25 (contract v14).** The lifecycle is keyed by `(epoch, spec_version)`, and the scoping above was right about the risk but wrong about the blast radius in a way that made the change much smaller. **Only `Aggregates` is re-keyed** (`MAX_AGGREGATES` 4 → 8): `Filings` and `FilingCount` stay epoch-keyed, so filing ids stay unique and **none of the ten 02 §6 filing events is touched** — only `RegistryEpochClosed` gains the version. Dropping the shared count at the first version's close is safe for a reason worth recording, because the counter looks like a hazard: `file` requires `now ≤ filing_window_end` and `close_epoch` requires `now > filing_window_end`, so **no filing can arrive for an epoch once any version has closed**. The two windows are disjoint by construction. The **fail-closed reader** landed, and refining it produced the sharpest finding: an unconditional refusal on a miss would have **wedged the chain**, because `close_epoch` deliberately refuses a never-filed epoch (anti-griefing) so most epochs never get a record at all and no snapshot could ever be taken. The rule is therefore two-way — no registry footprint ⇒ the neutral 1.0 is honest; a footprint that lacks *this* version ⇒ refuse — and 07 §7 was corrected from the absolute form I first wrote. **An independent review of the re-key then found a hole the re-key itself opened**, and it ran in both directions at once: because the first close drops the epoch-wide `FilingCount`, reaping that version while a sibling still held a non-terminal filing erased the epoch's only remaining evidence of having been filed, leaving the sibling permanently uncloseable *and* making the reader take the neutral branch for a version whose filings were still in storage. Closed by ordering the reap behind sibling closes (`ReapNotDue`), pinned by a mutation-checked regression — **and writing that regression turned up two more defects of the same family**, both mine. (i) The `try_state` partition asserted a filing is *either* counted-live *or* aggregated, which was exhaustive before versioning and is not now: the first close releases the epoch-wide count, so a sibling's filings are legitimately neither, and try-state failed on a healthy chain. The invariant is restated as its two real properties — never in two stages, never in none — with the third state recognised. (ii) The reader's evidence was scoped to the **epoch** rather than to the version, which stranded a version that legitimately has no filings: an incident filed under the sibling leaves an epoch footprint, so a version whose cohorts had nothing filed against them would refuse indefinitely unless a keeper cranked a close for a version with nothing to close — putting a safety read behind off-chain liveness for no gain. **SQ-175's consumer half landed with it**: `milestone_target` is a real per-version read of the frozen spec, and `cohort_exposure(Milestone, ·)` is determinable for the first time. Weights regenerated for four pallets with nine scoped acknowledgements; the `pallet_epoch` hand-edit trap (SQ-490) was re-spliced and the function set diffed before and after. |

| SQ-234 | **Entrenched enactment is a fixed 84 days, not four live epochs.** `min_enactment_period = 4 × 21 d` while `epoch.length` is governable 14–42 d, so at maximum epoch length the priced-second-opinion window is ~2 epochs. Pre-dates B1b; stock `pallet-referenda::TrackInfo` cannot schedule relative to epoch boundaries — needs a specified custom enactment mechanism or a 06 §2.1 wording ruling. | 06 §2.1/§2.4; 05 §3 | 2026-07-17 (B1b adversarial review) | **resolved 2026-07-26 — implemented as `4 × epoch.length`'s ceiling.** The 2026-07-21 ruling (four *actual* boundary crossings) stands; what changed is that the mechanics were verified, and they make the simplest implementation also the strongest. **Three facts settled the design.** (i) `pallet-referenda` reads the delay **once, at bake time** — `earliest_allowed = now + min_enactment_period` (vendored `schedule_enactment`) — so a delay derived from the *live* epoch length is still shaveable by a lengthening that lands after approval; `epoch.length`'s max-Δ 10 % / cooldown 2 epochs rate-limits that to roughly one boundary, not to zero. (ii) An exactly-four dispatch-time gate needs an approval-epoch anchor, and referenda exposes no on-confirm hook to record one — it would take a two-phase arm/apply surface across 06's authority matrix, new storage, and a scheduled dispatch that can fail and need re-attempt (a liveness surface) for the difference between "exactly 4" and "≥ 4". (iii) `epoch.length` is **kernel-bounded** (13 rule 7), so its whole metadata tuple — including the 42 d ceiling — is genesis-fixed and `amend_registry` refuses it. Sizing the delay at `4 × ceiling` (168 d) therefore guarantees ≥ 4 boundaries at **any** legal length, statically, with no new machinery: shortening epochs only adds boundaries. Sourced from `constitution_core::EPOCH_LENGTH_CEILING_BLOCKS`, the single home the registry ceiling is itself seeded from, and deliberately **not** the `fast-timing` arm — every 06 §2.1 track period stays at its release value in that build so governance windows cannot fire inside a minute-scale drill. **The cost is stated, not glossed:** at the 21 d default the delay doubles (84 → 168 d, ~210 d end to end), and it applies to every `entrenched`-class 13 §1 row in **both** directions — a *raise* of `att.bond` waits it out too. Accepted as the price of a guaranteed boundary count; a row whose adjustment latency outweighs its second opinion belongs in a different class, which is a 13-side decision. **Tests:** the track-table pin moves 84 → 168 and gains a derivation assertion (the delay must *equal* `4 × the ceiling constant`, not merely match a literal), plus a test reading `epoch.length`'s **live registry record** and asserting ≥ 4 boundaries at both its min and max — and that the row is `kernel_bounded`, since the whole guarantee rests on the ceiling being immutable.  **Codex review (PR #178) found three, all valid, all fixed or recorded.** (a) **P1 — the guarantee is conditional**: `epoch.tick` is permissionless, so elapsed blocks are not crossed epochs. The sizing is unchanged (nothing block-denominated can do better), but 06 §2.4 now states exactly what it delivers instead of claiming crossings, and the residual is **SQ-498** with its arm/apply design costed. My own sentence overclaimed; the reviewer was right to catch it. (b) **P1 — wrong home for the ceiling**: it went into `constitution-core` when `futarchy-primitives` already homes the matching *floor* (`PRODUCTION_MIN_EPOCH_LENGTH_BLOCKS`) — the symmetry I had noted in my own research and then ignored. Now `kernel::PRODUCTION_MAX_EPOCH_LENGTH_BLOCKS`, with the registry seed and the runtime both deriving from it and no runtime dependency on the constitution pallet for a kernel value. (c) **P2 — the exact-ratio assertion fails under `fast-timing`**, where the registry ceiling compresses while the delay deliberately does not; the cross-profile invariant is `4 × max <= delay`, with equality asserted only on the production profile.|

Substance: read together, those two 02 rules make the reserved bits **frozen zero for the life of the layout** — a future flag is a new appended field, never a redefinition of bits 3–31 — so a non-zero reserved bit is a record no conforming writer produced. Readers therefore **reject rather than mask** (masking would silently accept an unauthenticated writer's record), rejection MUST surface as degraded/unknown and never as healthy (for §3.2 neither "no newer release" nor "no security flag"; for §6.3 the series go absent, never zero), and readers MUST accept values **longer** than 168 bytes — which the shipped O5 reader already does. | SQ-285 | Should the dead-man **recovery epoch expose an exit for intake bonds**? Shipped behaviour closes `withdraw` for the whole recovery epoch: the legal guard is `proposal.epoch == CurrentEpoch`, recovery is a fresh index (resume increments the clock) and `submit` is refused throughout, so no proposal can satisfy it — a proposer whose bond is held cannot exit for ~1 epoch. Bounded deferral, not forfeiture: the bond stays held and withdrawal reopens when carry-forward re-anchors the proposal on the roll ending recovery. But G-1 argues an exit that only *releases* funds and advances nothing should not be gated on a liveness incident the proposer did not cause. Options: (a) ratify the deferral as-is; (b) relax `withdraw`'s epoch guard to accept any `Submitted` proposal while recovery is set, cancelling and refunding immediately; (c) re-anchor carried-forward proposals at the *start* of recovery rather than at the roll that ends it, which restores the guard without touching `withdraw`. (b) and (c) are code; (c) interacts with the intake-queue admission bound. | 05 §4.8 | 2026-07-20 (B1 · Codex P2 review of PR #114) | **resolved 2026-07-20 (ratified as shipped; delegated ruling).** Option (a): the deferral stands. 05 §4.8 now states it normatively. The reasoning that closed it is that the G-1 test was misapplied when this row was raised — G-1 constrains what the protocol *does* on a failure path, and declining to process an exit is **inaction**: no bond is forfeited, no claim is created, the proposer's position is preserved exactly, and withdrawal reopens on the roll that ends recovery. Force-rejection *is* the status quo (the payload does not dispatch either way), and letting a mandate wait would need maturity/grace extension machinery that exists only for the dead-man (05 §4.8), not for a freeze — without it a waiting mandate just expires mid-freeze, the same terminal outcome reached later and with a worse bond disposition. 09 §1.2(10) is **not** left vacuous: the keeper sweep is per-proposal and bounded, so between activation and the sweep reaching a given mandate there is a real window in which `execute()` must refuse. **Precedence:** the freeze wins over a concurrent dead-man pause. The two answer different failures — the dead-man is a *liveness* pause that preserves state, `PB-LEDGER-FREEZE` a machine-checked *solvency* anomaly (I-4 drift) in which backing is in doubt — and a stalled clock is not a reason to keep live proposals standing over a possibly-unbacked ledger. This is the shipped ordering (`crates/epoch-core/src/lib.rs`: the sweep precedes the dead-man hold), so the code comment added with SQ-98 is now backed by spec text. No code change. |

| SQ-135 | 15 §4.5 demands "a clean `cargo-audit` pass under the 01 §9 exact-pin regime", but the pinned stable2603 tree carries 24 RustSec vulnerabilities (16× `wasmtime 35.0.0`, `hickory-proto`, `rustls-webpki 0.101.7`, `ring 0.16.20`, `tracing-subscriber =0.3.19` — the last pinned by `sc-tracing 45.0.0` itself) with **no fix available inside the pin regime**. B8 implements the only workable mechanism: per-entry-annotated `.cargo/audit.toml` ignores (each names the pinning SDK component + the obligation to clear it at the next stable2603 maintenance bump), keeper workspace audited with no inherited exceptions, and the full waived-ID list disclosed in every release manifest. Ratify this waiver mechanism (or amend 15 §4.5 to name it); the standing obligation to re-triage at every SDK bump stands regardless.. **Re-triaged 2026-07-17** against the 25 open Dependabot alerts: the waiver list is *exactly* precise (1:1 with the 23 firing ids — zero stale, zero missing) and every entry is still pin-forced, with `cargo update --precise` attempted per family and the verbatim blocker recorded. Two refinements: (1) `lru` RUSTSEC-2026-0002 correctly needs **no** exception (`informational = "unsound"` → an allowed warning), so the gate is green rather than under-configured; (2) the mechanism had a **structural hole** — RustSec is a strict subset of the GitHub Advisory DB for crates.io, so `yamux` GHSA-vxx9-2994-q338 (HIGH, remote panic) was invisible to it entirely; closed by the GHSA-only leg under **SQ-219**. The *"remove at the next stable2603 maintenance bump"* obligation every entry carries now has a named owner: **B11** — **executed 2026-07-17 (D-19 stable2606 line move)**: from-scratch re-triage deleted the 16 `wasmtime` entries; the 7 survivors + the yamux GHSA entry were each re-proven pin-forced on the new lockfile and re-annotated under per-family exit criteria (libp2p-forced / litep2p-forced / sc-tracing-forced) | 15 §4.5; 01 §9 | 2026-07-17 (B8; re-triaged by B11) | **resolved 2026-07-20 (B5 ratification; waiver mechanism ratified into 15 §4.5).** The tension is real and now stated: the exact-pin regime and a clean advisory gate genuinely conflict when a pinned SDK component forces a vulnerable version, so "clean" means clean **under a declared, annotated exception set** subject to five normative conditions — per-entry annotation naming the forcing component *and* a per-family exit criterion, recorded pin-forced proof, mechanical expiry plus from-scratch re-triage at every train bump, blast-radius containment for workspaces outside the SDK closure, and disclosure in every **publishable** release manifest. Waiver count is explicitly never a gate. Deliberately **source-agnostic**: which advisory databases are normative stays open as SQ-219 (batch B6), so this ruling cannot pre-empt it. Verified against the tree (7 annotated ignores + 1 GHSA waiver, keeper audited from its own root, `bleavit.supply-chain.v2` carried in the manifest); one nuance recorded rather than ratified — keeper isolation rests on cargo-audit's CWD config discovery, contained by the version pin, not by a structural guarantee. |
| SQ-136 | 15 §5 requires artifacts "published … and mirrored content-addressed (Arweave)" before a release is publishable, but CI holds no keys (12/O1) — the ordering is circular if "mirrored" must precede publication. B8 implements a two-step: the tag release is created **prerelease** with notes stating it is not canonical until an operator attaches mirror evidence (JSON mapping each SHA-256 → Arweave TXID; documented in `tools/release/README.md`); the manifest carries `mirror.status: pending`. It does now: (a) CI publishes the artifact set as a **prerelease** whose notes state it is not canonical and whose manifest records the mirror duty outstanding; (b) an operator attaches mirror evidence mapping every content digest to its Arweave TXID; (c) the release is promoted to canonical. **"Publishable" in the gating rule is step (a)** — what a runtime release must clear to ship at all — while canonical status, which frontend releases and §1.4 repoints depend on, requires (c). The mutable-host independence §5 asserts is therefore preserved by (c), not by (a). Ratified as shipped: the pipeline creates a visible prerelease and every manifest carries `mirror.status: pending` unconditionally. |

Both cranks therefore land on identical ledger state; previously a race decided whether Accept-branch holders recovered ½ (par void) or nothing (Reject-branch resolution). Par void is also the only self-consistent choice: the freeze halts `market.crank_observe`, so `reject_to_measurement` would have sent proposals to await a score the freeze itself prevents producing. `dead_man_armed` and `guards.process_hold` were deliberately left in the decision chain (the 05 §4.8 dead-man asymmetry is intentional). Precedence note: the freeze check now precedes the static guards, so a freeze forgoes the 10 % `!preimage_ok` slash — accepted, and conservative in the G-1 direction (no confiscation during a machine-checked solvency emergency; cf. the SQ-191 ruling that confiscation requires a verified culpable act). Disambiguating requires carrying the vault outcome in the transition record (T20 voids; T10 resolves into measurement), which is a modelling change owed its own pass. The reason for the binding is now commented in the model itself. |

| SQ-517 | **Is the whole permissionless keeper-crank family in scope of `PB-LEDGER-FREEZE`?** Raised by the Track E spec audit as a *major*, and filed rather than coded because the two texts genuinely disagree and the answer moves pre-existing behavior. 06 §6.3's Effect freezes "**all** ledger calls … and all market calls … both inflow and outflow, because during an unattributed drift either direction can be the exploit", and its live-list (reconciliation crank, guardian calls, values referenda, oracle/dispute calls) names none of the cranks; 03 §5.4 gives `sweep_redemption_fees` preconditions "**none**". **My analysis, for whoever rules.** The substantive case for freezing is strong: `sweep_redemption_fees` rests on L-7's premise that the accrual is *surplus above* the maintained liability, and a freeze is admissible exactly when the reconciliation crank has proved `liability > custody` — so the premise is false precisely when the crank would run, and the sweep removes real backing. `sweep_revenue` likewise redeems sovereign escrow out to `POL`/`MAIN`. Neither is a settlement call, so §6.3's carve-out ("a freeze must not strand a terminal vault transition") does not reach them: both run strictly *after* terminality, and freezing them defers cleanup rather than stranding anything — POL merely stays committed, which is fail-static. **But it is not this milestone's call to make.** `pallets/market/src/tests.rs::ledger_freeze_blocks_trading_but_not_recovery_and_renews_once` *deliberately* asserts that `sweep_revenue` and `reap` succeed under an active freeze — a tested posture predating Track E (B10/E1) — and `sweep_dust`/`sweep_dust_baseline`/`reap` are unfrozen on the same reading, so a ruling has to settle the family, not two calls. A revenue-instruments PR is the wrong place to reverse an emergency-brake semantic | 06 §6.3; 03 §5.4; 04 §2; 15 I-4 | 2026-07-29 | **resolved 2026-07-29 (milestone E4) — both Track-E cranks are frozen; 06 §6.3, 03 §5.4/L-7 and 04 §2 amended to say so.** The ruling needed no values judgement in the end, because L-7 supplies a proof rather than a preference: its bound is `RedemptionFeesAccrued ≤ balance(sovereign) − TotalEscrowed − held_deposits − min_balance`, and the I-4 drift flag — the *sole* admission condition for `PB-LEDGER-FREEZE` — asserts exactly `TotalEscrowed + held_deposits > balance(sovereign)`. The bound is therefore **negative under precisely the state that authorizes a freeze**, so "moves surplus, never escrow" is a theorem about the healthy state and not a property of the crank, and `Preservation::Preserve` does not supply the missing guarantee (it protects `min_balance` and is indifferent to escrow). `sweep_revenue` fails for the sibling reason: its fee leg redeems through the ledger's *internal* path, which carries no `Frozen` check, so it would collect the protocol's own claim out of a short sovereign while every claimant's `redeem` is refused. Freezing both **strands nothing** — neither effects a terminal transition, both are retryable, and the value stays fully collateralized in place — which is what distinguishes them from the settlement calls 06 §6.3 deliberately leaves live; the cost is an NAV-recognition delay bounded by the freeze's own ≤ 28-day ceiling. The guard sits **after** `sweep_revenue`'s idempotence early-return, so a freeze never retroactively changes what an already-swept book answers (asserted, not just commented). `reap` is delayed transitively and inertly (it discards only worthless residue); `sweep_dust*` stays live and unchanged — it is the terminal-vault cleanup the settlement carve-out covers, its residue is a liability transfer to INSURANCE rather than a treasury payout, and it is already behind a one-year archive delay. Both new tests are mutation-proven: with the guards removed each fails on its own `Frozen` assertion. **The superseded reading, kept because the process lesson is the transferable part:** I reverted a correct code change because `ledger_freeze_blocks_trading_but_not_recovery_and_renews_once` appeared to assert *deliberately* that `sweep_revenue` survives a freeze, "a tested posture predating Track E". Both halves are false: `git log -S` shows the `sweep()` helper and its call inside that test were added **today, by E1 (`3f716ca`)**, as mechanical plumbing so the test still passed once `reap` gained its swept-marker precondition — not as a ruling, and not predating anything. No Decision-log entry rules on freeze scope for cranks. So 06 §6.3 governs unopposed: "**all** ledger calls … and all market calls error `Frozen`", with an enumerated live-list (reconciliation crank, guardian calls, values referenda, oracle/dispute calls) that excludes both, and a settlement carve-out that cannot reach them because they run strictly *after* terminality. **Narrowed scope:** the two Track-E cranks (`sweep_revenue`, `sweep_redemption_fees`) are this PR's to fix. `reap` and `sweep_dust`/`sweep_dust_baseline` are pre-existing behaviour from B1b and stay here — though note the coupling, which makes the question less urgent than it looks: with `sweep_revenue` frozen, `reap` cannot proceed anyway, since it requires the swept marker |

Their expectations encode the pre-fix routing. The routing itself is unchanged and correct — the slash still lands in INSURANCE, and §1.2's above-target surplus then overflows to `MAIN` in the same transaction — so the end state is INSURANCE at `T_ins` and `MAIN` credited, and it is the assertions that are stale. So there is no code on `main` to fix: a separate PR would have had to be *stacked* on #196, which is precisely the configuration already recorded as making a PR's weight gate blind to every function its own base introduces. The size argument was real but did not survive the provenance check, and size is not a reason to put a change where it cannot correctly be built. **Landed here.** `note_insurance_inflow()` is called from both USDC slash adapters, best-effort and each inside its own `with_storage_layer` — that layer is load-bearing rather than defensive: `overflow_insurance` credits `main_usdc` *before* moving custody and relies on the dispatch to undo the credit if custody refuses, so swallowing the error without a layer would keep the credit and overstate NAV against custody that never moved. | SQ-521 | **CodeQL `rust/cleartext-logging` fires high-severity on a differential-test helper, and it is a naming false positive — but the repo has no CodeQL waiver mechanism.** Alert 18 on `crates/conditional-ledger-core/tests/differential_vectors.rs:143`, "This operation writes account to a log file", introduced by `1f81a31` (E2/E3/E4) and blocking #196's `CodeQL` check. **The evidence that it is spurious is conclusive and structural.** That line is `other => panic!("unknown vector holder class: {other}")`, the fallthrough of a three-arm match over the literals `alice`/`bob`/`carol`; the taint source is line 273's `string(args, "account")`, a JSON key in the committed vector corpus. The file contains **seven structurally identical helpers** — `unknown branch`, `unknown gate`, `unknown scalar side`, `unknown position kind`, `unknown position family`, `unhandled vector operation`, `unknown Python ledger error class` — and **only** the one whose field happens to be named `account` is flagged. Same shape seven times, one alert: the query is keying on the identifier name, not on any property of the data. CodeQL classifies the instance itself as `["test"]`, the values are three hardcoded labels in a public committed fixture, and the binary never ships in the runtime. **Why the code fix is the wrong answer**, having considered it: removing the interpolation would make one of seven identical helpers strictly worse at diagnosing a corpus/replayer mismatch, for a reason no future reader could infer from the code — and renaming the `"account"` field is not available either, since that key is part of the shared vector schema the reference model writes (changing it means regenerating the corpus to dodge a heuristic). Contorting code to satisfy a false positive is precisely what this repo's annotated-waiver culture (`ghsa-waivers.toml`, `generated-weight-overrides.toml`, `weight-preservation.toml`) exists to avoid. **Why it is not simply waivable either:** CodeQL here runs under GitHub **default setup**, which has no in-repo config file, and inline `// codeql[rule-id]` suppressions are honored by the CodeQL CLI/SARIF path but **not** by default setup (github/codeql#11427, #9298; the `advanced-security/dismiss-alerts` Action exists to bridge exactly this gap). So the two mechanisms that would actually clear it are both repo-administration acts: dismiss alert 18 as a false positive, or move CodeQL to **advanced setup** with a config excluding test paths — the latter also giving the repo a reviewable, in-tree waiver surface consistent with every other gate here | `crates/conditional-ledger-core/tests/differential_vectors.rs`; GitHub code scanning default setup | 2026-07-29 | **resolved 2026-07-29 — alert 18 dismissed as `used in tests`; and my first recommendation was wrong, which is the part worth keeping.** The user delegated the call, and working it through reversed it. I had recommended **advanced setup with test paths excluded** on the grounds that it is durable and prevents the next spurious alert. That reasoning ignored what it costs: excluding test paths permanently blinds CodeQL to an entire category of code **across the whole repository** in order to settle one naming false positive. Dismissing a single alert is surgical, reversible, uses the mechanism GitHub designed for exactly this, and **preserves full scanning coverage on test code**. For financial infrastructure the narrow action is the safer one, so the broad remedy was the worse remedy — I had ranked durability above blast radius. It also avoids touching a default-setup/branch-protection surface mid-PR, where a check-name change could have blocked every PR in the repo, but that is a secondary benefit and not the reason. **Reason chosen deliberately:** `used in tests` rather than `false positive`, because it is the more precise of the two and it **self-invalidates** — it ties the waiver to a fact that would change (the code being a test) rather than to a standing judgement about whether logging an account is safe. If this helper ever moves out of `tests/`, the stated ground stops holding and the alert should be reopened; that is the property an auditor needs and a `false positive` dismissal would not give. The API caps dismissal comments at 280 characters, so the comment states the finding and points here: **PLAN.md is the durable in-tree record**, which is the same division of labour every other waiver in this repo uses. No code changed — see the seven-siblings argument in the question column |
| SQ-522 | **`pallet_epoch` weights understated on `main`, and three milestones of drift had accumulated inside the gate's documented advisory window.** Found while regenerating for SQ-518 at the committed 50x20 fidelity. On the merge base `af2e5a0`, `pallet_welfare.rs` declares `Welfare::Snapshots (r:61 w:60)` while `pallet_epoch.rs` declares `(r:21 w:20)` — the same storage bound, the same runtime, two committed weight files disagreeing. `pallet_epoch`'s benchmark is not seeding a smaller fixture: `seed_welfare_retirement_history` reads `BenchmarkSnapshots::iter_keys().count()`, which the assembled-runtime helper populates *at its retained capacity*, so the fixture scales with `MAX_SNAPSHOTS` and `r:21` is simply the pre-MAX-01 bound of 20. Regeneration also picks up **A14** (`Welfare::BlockProductionEpoch` and `CollatorAuthorshipEpoch`, `r:0 w:2` each, absent from the committed file) and **E1** (`Constitution::Params` 41 -> 43 and 34 -> 36 for the `ledger.rdm_fee`/`ledger.min_split` overlay, plus `RedemptionFeesAccrued`). Direction is **understatement**, the one direction 15 §4.5 says weights must never err in. **Why no per-commit gate saw it, stated from the code rather than the doc:** `regenerate-weights.py` buckets a drift as hard only when `matches or not has_components` — `matches` being run fidelity equal to the committed header's. These epoch functions are component-bearing (`Estimated: 183055 + n * (30754 +/-57)`), and the `benchmark-smoke` job runs `--steps 2 --repeat 1` against a 50x20 header, so every one of these deltas landed in **advisory** and printed without failing. That is the *documented* tradeoff, not a defect in the gate — a 2-point fit can lose a linear term outright, so hard-gating component functions at low fidelity would produce false failures. The consequence is the part worth recording: the hard gate for these is the release-blocking `Component weights at committed fidelity` job in `release.yml`, which runs only at tag time, so this drift would first have surfaced as a **failed release** rather than a failed PR | 15 §4.5; `tools/ci/regenerate-weights.py`; `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (`benchmark-smoke`) | 2026-07-29 | **resolved incidentally 2026-07-29 (milestone E4) — the corrected weights ship with SQ-518, and the fix was not optional.** Regenerating `pallet_epoch` for SQ-518's seam necessarily re-measures the whole pallet, so the accumulated drift came with it; excluding it would have meant hand-editing generated weight functions, which the 15 §4.5 generated-weight purity gate forbids outright. `check-weight-regression.py` passes: none of the epoch deltas crossed its 10 % worst-case limit against the merge base, so no acknowledgement was required for them. **What stays open is the question, not this instance** — whether a cheap per-commit run should hard-gate the *storage* dimensions of component-bearing functions at their component high, since reads/writes at a fixed fixture are structural rather than statistical and do not have ref_time's 127 % spread. That is a change to the gate's own design and belongs to whoever revisits SQ-490's regime, not to a revenue-instruments PR |
| SQ-523 | **The E3 fee handler adds unweighted storage work to every USDC-paying extrinsic — and the same investigation found the USDC fee path is inert at genesis.** Raised as **P1** by the #196 round-4 Codex review. `UsdcFeesToMain::handle_credit` (`runtime/bleavit-runtime/src/configs.rs:374-390`) resolves the credit into `MAIN`'s asset account **and** mutates `FutarchyTreasury::PendingMainCredit`, inside `pallet_asset_tx_payment`'s `ChargeAssetTxPayment` extension, while `type WeightInfo = ()` leaves the extension charging the SDK's own reference-runtime measurement. The SDK weight is also the exact post-dispatch weight, so there is no later correction: roughly two reads and two writes per USDC-paid extrinsic go uncharged, and a block filled with such calls can exceed its declared execution/PoV budget. Understatement is the one direction 15 §4.5 forbids. The runtime-registry comment claiming these costs are "carried by the extrinsic base weight" was true before E3 and is now stale — the base extrinsic weight is a measured constant that cannot know about a runtime's custom `HandleCredit`. **Practical severity is bounded by a second finding, which is the more interesting one:** `fee.vit_usdc` is **not** a genesis-seeded key (absent from `constitution_core::genesis_params()` and from `tools/limit-coverage/genesis-keys.json`), and `LiveFeeConversion` fails closed without it — so on a genesis chain the entire USDC fee path is **inert** and this handler is unreachable until governance sets a rate. The defect is real but latent, and it arms exactly when that rate is set | 15 §4.5; 08 §9; `runtime/bleavit-runtime/src/configs.rs`; `runtime/bleavit-runtime/src/lib.rs` benchmark registry | 2026-07-29 | **resolved 2026-07-30.** Fixed by benchmarking `pallet_asset_tx_payment` **in this runtime** and binding `type WeightInfo` to the generated artifact. The prior attempt aborted on `test_run`'s `.unwrap()` and I had guessed at why; this time the error was **instrumented** rather than inferred — `test_run` is not benchmark-gated, so a plain runtime test drives the extension in the same `development` genesis the bencher builds. It reported `Invalid(Payment)` for *bare* and for *rate-only*, and `OK` once the caller held USDC: the fixture needed exactly two preconditions, the governed rate and a funded payer, and neither is a genesis given. Both now live in `AssetTxBenchmarkHelper::setup_balances_and_pool`, and `create_asset_id_parameter` returns `usdc_location()` because `LiveFeeConversion` rejects every other asset — the stock synthetic id would have measured the conversion's **`Err` arm**, a cheap early return, and weighted the paying path with it. **What the measurement showed is worse than the estimate in this row.** The SDK's `()` charged 5 reads / **2 writes** / **3,675 B** estimated proof; the real path measures 5 reads / **4 writes** / **7,404 B** — a **2.01x PoV understatement**, +3,729 B on *every* USDC-paid extrinsic, against a 3,932,160 B normal-class budget. The row's "roughly two reads and two writes" was right on writes and silent on the dimension that actually bounds a parachain block. The measured storage lines are exactly the E3 seams: `Constitution::Params` r:1 (the rate), `ForeignAssets::Asset` r:1 w:1 + `ForeignAssets::Account` r:2 w:2 (withdraw plus the resolve into `MAIN`), `FutarchyTreasury::PendingMainCredit` r:1 w:1 (recognition). **The spec was also wrong, and that is the durable half:** 15 §4.5 mandated benchmarks "for every call and hook" — a transaction extension is neither, so the surface this defect lived on was outside the mandate's scope entirely. Amended under R-1 (see the Decision log): the mandate now names extensions, and a new normative bullet states why an understatement here is worse than for a call (the post-dispatch refund is **self-referential** — it subtracts the same `WeightInfo` function it charged, so on the charged path it is identically zero — and the weight is charged per *extrinsic* rather than per feature-user, so the error scales with block occupancy) and requires upstream fixtures to be re-pointed when this runtime narrows their admissible inputs. Verification: three fixtures generated at the committed 50x20 fidelity, the all-32-pallet drift gate, and a named runtime test (`the_usdc_fee_extension_benchmark_fixture_measures_the_paying_path`) that pins **both** preconditions plus the assertion that the benchmarked path really moves custody and NAV — so a future break surfaces as a named test failure rather than as an unexplained weights-pipeline abort

| SQ-552 | **The 09 §1.2 ↔ 11 §11.5 diff that both documents mandate does not exist, and it fails on five rows.** 09 §1.2's 13-item dispatch check list is "normative and canonical"; 11 §11.5 "MUST mirror it item-for-item"; 15's contract tests are said to diff them. Parsing both: 13 backend items against 14 frontend rows, nine one-to-one. Backend item 1 maps to FE 1–2; item 10 to FE 11–12; backend items 12–13 have no FE precondition; and **FE row 14 (`DescriptorLeadTime`) is an `apply_authorized_upgrade` precondition per 09 §2.2, not an `execute` one** — so it can wrongly block a valid `execute`. Separately, 09 §1.2(11) names `Rejected(BadPreimage)`, but `BadPreimage` is a `pallet_execution_guard::Error` and **not** a member of the frozen `RejectReason` set: that terminal state cannot be constructed, the runtime returns `Err`, and the proposal stays `Queued` until T15 `Expired` — so clients may treat a still-live queued mandate as terminal. One further row: 05 §5.5's `Valid fail` publishes `HurdleNotMet` where normative §5.4 returns `ConvergenceFailed`. **Ruling needed:** add the variant to the frozen set (contract bump) or change the disposition | 09 §1.2, §2.2; 11 §11.5; 05 §5.4–§5.5; 02 §4 | 2026-08-01 | **Resolved 2026-08-03 (F6), four rulings.** **(1) The mirror is over checks, not items.** 09 §1.2 items 12–13 are *dispatch* and *record* — the effects of passing, with nothing to pre-check — so the FE mirrors items **1–11**, and two of those deliberately expand into two rows each (BE 1 → queued/window; BE 10 → gate flags/dead-man). 11 backend checks, 13 frontend rows, and the 15 §4.x contract test diffs checks to checks over the stated mapping rather than list lengths; a length diff could only be satisfied by inventing frontend rows for effects, which is how a client acquires a precondition the runtime does not have. **(2) FE row 14 deleted.** 09 §2.2 binds `DescriptorLeadTime` to `system.apply_authorized_upgrade`, where `authorized_at` is the block of `UpgradeAuthorized` — which the guard emits *as a result of* a successful `execute`. At `execute` dispatch the timestamp does not exist for that proposal, so the row was unsatisfiable or reading an earlier authorization's clock; it could block a valid `execute`. Its home is §11.8.4, tightened at the same time to read the stored **`PendingUpgrade.applicable_at`** rather than re-derive it: §2.2's SafetyFilter denies on that field, and a client re-deriving it from a separately-read registry value would refuse or admit on a number the filter is not using. **(3) `Rejected(BadPreimage)` → the disposition changes, not the frozen set.** Verified against the shipped runtime: `RejectReason` has no such variant, and `pallet_execution_guard` returns `Error::BadPreimage` inside `with_storage_layer`, so the run rolls back and the proposal stays `Queued` until T15 `Expired`. 09 §1.2(11) now says that — the same correction SQ-163 made to item 4, for the same reason: a dispatch-time check that *errors* is not a transition. One difference is now stated for clients, because it is the one that misleads: a malformed preimage is **permanent** where an unpassed referendum is transient, so the mandate is doomed while its on-chain state still reads `Queued`. Recording it terminally instead — which item 7's own retry-bounding reasoning would favour — needs a `RejectReason` variant and therefore an integration-contract bump plus runtime work, so it is **left open as SQ-578** rather than smuggled into a frontend milestone. **(4) 05 §5.5's `Valid fail` row was wrong in two directions.** §5.4 evaluates steps 6–8 and dispatches on the **triple**; the row treated them as short-circuiting. With 6 and 7 disagreeing the engine returns **`Extend`** (or `SecondExtensionFailed`), not a hurdle rejection at all; with 8 also failing it returns **`ConvergenceFailed`**, because an unconverged series is not evidence the hurdle was genuinely missed. `HurdleNotMet` is correct only for `full_pass = tail_pass = false ∧ converged`. One row replaced by five. |

| SQ-561 | **The 07 §3 permanent ban is defeated by arithmetic: fill the retained-record store with ejections and the next ejection re-registers at full stake with a clean ladder.** `MAX_REPORTER_RECORDS = MAX_REPORTERS = 64` and the eviction rule correctly refuses to drop an ejection, so the store can reach a state where `upsert_reporter_record` returns `false`. `record_reporter_offense` then emits `ReporterRecordsFull` and **releases the seat anyway** — which it must, since G-1 forbids a full table from aborting a values-track verdict. Once no ban can be recorded, an unrecorded account is indistinguishable from a dropped ban, so entry closes rather than admitting one; seated reporters are untouched, so the live set keeps serving; and the only escape is a CODE change enlarging the store — the right venue, since the size is a consensus constant whose growth is a PoV cost. Regression test drives the **real** ejection path (`a_saturated_ban_store_closes_entry_instead_of_re_admitting_the_ejected`) and fails if either half is reverted |

The structural form: **the cheapest governance to deny is the class Bleavit subsidizes least**, because the attack cost tracks `pol.b` and PARAM's is smallest. It also verifies the Track N plan's unsourced ≈ 3,000 USDC/epoch estimate — 2,786 for CODE by an unrelated route, within 7 %. **Not exploitable today**: `svc.client_bond` is `[VERIFY]`-unset so `admit_client` refuses everyone and the service is inert — this is N14 scope, not an incident | 14 TH-72; 16 §8.1/§8.4; 13 §1 (`svc.fee_bps`) / §2 (`SVC_FEE_FLOOR_USDC`); 08 §7 | 2026-08-03 (N14 derivation) | **open — figures withdrawn 2026-08-03 by adversarial review; the code-verified half stands.** An independent read-only Codex pass (`gpt-5.6-luna`, `max`) was asked to refute five claims and refuted three. **(i) The depth arithmetic double-counted.** `pol.b` is quoted *per branch*, i.e. per book, and `parity_depth_cash` multiplied by a further 2 for "the question's two books" — every cash figure was 2× high. Verified independently before accepting. The error direction was **against this row's own conclusion**: it inflated the attacker's cost and understated the hole. It also regressed a figure already computed correctly by hand earlier the same day (1,589 for CODE), and it walked past the suite's only arithmetic guard, which pinned `b` versus `b·ln 2` and not the branch count. **(ii) The harm normalization smuggled an assumption**: every ratio divides by the hosted attack's measured harm while treating `intake_denial`'s harm as 1.0 — total denial — which is stated nowhere and justified nowhere, so each ratio is wrong by 1/H_I. **(iii) The capital charge is lower-order, not conservative.** Worst-case LMSR maker loss *is* the posted cash, ≈ 348× the carrying cost the model counted; excluding a term two orders of magnitude larger than the one included does not make a figure conservative, it makes it not a figure. **Consequently the uplift targets (1,710 / 2,487 / 1,752 / 1,002) and the ratios (3.16× / 2.79× / 1.63× / 1.23×) are WITHDRAWN and MUST NOT be carried into 13 or 16.** What survives is the code-verified half — a flat 393 USDC buys arbitrary depth — which rests on the registration path, not on any of the broken arithmetic. **Both remaining claims came back REFUTED (2026-08-03), and between them they take the row's headline and its anchor.** **(iv) 'A flat 393 USDC buys arbitrary depth' is false, and this row's own arithmetic contradicted it.** The *fee* is flat in depth — `declared_stake = 1` collapses the rate leg and the 393 floor binds however large `b` is — but depth is not bought with the fee: registration derives `escrow = 2·seed_headroom(b) = 2·b·ln 2`, the funder must hold it, and it is checked against `phase3.tvl_cap`, so depth tops out at `b ≈ 1,442,695` USDC (independently reproduced). The surviving statement is narrow: **the fee does not scale with depth; the capital requirement does**, and whether flat fees on TVL-bounded depth is itself a defect is now an open question rather than an asserted one. **(v) The equalization benchmark is invalid because the harms are incommensurable.** `intake_denial` fills the 64-entry queue so new submissions get `IntakeFull` — it blocks *admission* and cannot block the decision call for a proposal already in `Trading`, which is precisely what depth-thinning attacks. Crowding a queue and starving a live decision are different harms, so the cheaper is not a price for the other; `cheapest_priced_denial_channel` is **removed rather than re-pointed**, since `slot_capture` is closer in kind but is a different strategy at a different price and choosing between them needs evidence that does not exist. **Net: N14's case for demand-responsive pricing now rests entirely on *allocation* — sniping and first-come-first-served under contention, which needs no threat-cost benchmark — and the separate claim that hosted denial is *underpriced* is unsubstantiated and must not be asserted.** The module keeps the refutations rather than deleting them, because each is a way the service looked cheaper or more dangerous than it is. **The review's side finding is now SQ-575 and is larger than this row.** N14 owns the repair, and the repair is larger than the milestone assumed: occupancy-and-velocity pricing governs *allocation and sniping*, but one slot holds unlimited depth, so the fee also needs a **depth-proportional leg**. Two mechanisms, two jobs. Caveats travel with the figures: they rest on the proportional-to-depth flow model whose error direction 16 §8.4 records as unsafe (a better venue needs less depth ⇒ cheaper still), and they exclude the attacker's adverse-selection losses (⇒ dearer). Directional, not a bound either way |

Sixth instance of the family: SQ-552, SQ-577, SQ-580, SQ-581, SQ-585, this. **Ruling needed:** freeze `Market.MarketProtocolAccounts` (a contract bump, and a per-recipient storage read on every transfer), **or** publish the domain-separated `AccountId32` derivation 02 §13 v8 already asserts ("canonical book/fee addresses occupy a domain-separated namespace classified as protocol custody before creation and after reap") so membership is *derivable* with no read — which is cheaper and matches the durable property, but only if the namespace test and `contains_key` agree in both directions, which nothing currently checks | 11 §11.5; 02 §7.4, §13 v8 | 2026-08-04 | open |
