| V-88 | **FE-P4 (artifact-size half): smoldot 3.3.2 is 2.23 MiB gzipped, and `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` is load-bearing rather than defensive** | 10 §9.3, §4.1; 12 §5.1; INV-FE-1 | measured 2026-08-03 from the lockfile-pinned package | 10 §9.3 budgets *"smoldot WASM (worker, lazy) ≤ 3.5 MB gz **[VERIFY artifact size — FE-P4]**"*. Measured from `smoldot@3.3.2` as installed: the bytecode ships as **four JavaScript modules carrying zlib-compressed, base64-encoded string literals** — not as a `.wasm` file — totalling 3,082,260 B raw, **2,333,920 B gzip (2.23 MiB)** and 2,312,719 B brotli. **Within budget, with 1.31 MiB of headroom.** Two consequences the number alone does not give. **(1) The CSP directive is necessary, not cautious.** The browser path is `WebAssembly.compile(zlibInflate(trustedBase64Decode(wasmBase64)))` (`dist/mjs/bytecode-browser.js:34`) — a **buffer** compile, not `instantiateStreaming` from a URL. Chrome-family CSP requires `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` in `script-src` for buffer-based compilation, so 12 §5.1's `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'` is what lets the light client start at all in the majority browser. Dropping it would produce `FE-BOOT-004` on every Chrome load — a total INV-FE-1 failure — **while leaving every test in this repository green**, because nothing here executes under a CSP. That is worth a release gate of its own (F13's CSP-diff leg) rather than a comment. **(2) "Lazy" means a dynamic `import()` of a JS chunk**, not a `fetch` of a wasm asset, so the load is governed by `script-src` and never by the §5.1 `connect-src` allowlist — which also means the bundler must not be allowed to inline those four modules into the entry chunk, or the §9.3 lazy-load line becomes false without any budget number changing. **Still open in FE-P4:** per-instance memory (the §9.4 mobile budget's named 2 × ≤ 120 MB line), real sync latency, the 20 blk/s ingest anchor, measured proof sizes and mobile CPU — all of which need the device lab the gate names, and none of which this measurement touches. |
| V-87 | **FE-P1 (10 §5.2): PAPI 2.1.8's compatibility surface, names and semantics** | 10 §5.2, §3.2, §5.1; INV-FE-12 | verified 2026-08-03 by pinned-source reading; enum ordering pinned executably | 10 §5.2 left the compat API as `[VERIFY exact PAPI 2.x names/semantics — FE-P1]`. Answered from the lockfile-pinned tree, same method as V-82. **(1)** The surface is `(await api.getStaticApis()).compat[group][pallet][member]` over groups `tx`/`constants`/`apis`/`view`/`query`/`event` (`types-BJAMtGIT.d.ts:775–791`) — there is **no** `getCompatibilityToken()`; that was the 1.x shape, and looking for it is how a reader concludes the API is missing. **(2)** `compat` is typed `Safe extends true ? {…} : unknown`, so it exists on `getTypedApi(descriptors)` and **not** on `getUnsafeApi()`, whose own docstring says it \"does not provide any runtime compatibility checks protection\". **(3)** `isCompatible(from = CompatibilityLevel.BackwardsCompatible)` — `compatibility/compatibility.js:27` defines `getIsApiCompatible(currentLevel) => (target = BackwardsCompatible) => currentLevel >= target`, so **`Partial` reports `false` by default**. The client must therefore not pass its own threshold; doing so is a second opinion about safety with no basis, and passing `Partial` would silently widen what counts as signable. **(4)** A surface absent from the runtime yields the `inOutIncompat` singleton (`if (!dest.entry)`) — `Incompatible`, `isCompatible: () => false` — so absence is *detectable* and fails closed, which is what INV-FE-12 and the 10 §5.2 classifier need. **The trap, and why the probe takes a `compat` object rather than a client:** when no descriptors are supplied at all the helper reports the **value side as `identical`** (`value: user ? incompatible : identical`), which reads as \"fully compatible\" while nothing was compared. **(5)** Storage, runtime APIs and view fns carry `args`/`value` and **no top-level `level`**; PAPI computes their verdict as `min(args.level, value.level)`, and a consumer reading `helper.level` on those gets `undefined`. The numeric enum (`Incompatible 0 < Partial 1 < BackwardsCompatible 2 < Identical 3`) is now pinned **executably** — `tests/descriptors` imports PAPI's real enum and asserts both the naming and the ordering, because the ordering is what `isCompatible` compares and a renumbering would turn `Partial` into a pass. **Not verified:** that these structural shapes still match PAPI's, since nothing constructs a `TypedApi` until F6 wires `createClient` — the same exposure `topology.ts` closes with an assignability binding, and the same fix applies when the client lands. |

| V-85 | **A chainHead operation event arriving before its `started` response was dropped, hanging the read forever** | 10 §4.2 | found + fixed 2026-08-03 by the recorded-transcript provider (F3) | The `started` response and the operation's own follow-subscription events are separate messages; `await`ing the former yields to the microtask queue, so `operationStorageDone` can be delivered **before** the handler waiting for it is registered. The transport dropped it and the promise never settled. Worth recording for the failure mode as much as the bug: a hung read is indistinguishable on screen from a slow chain, so it produces a bug report about the network. Fixed with a bounded orphan buffer drained at registration — bounded because the buffer is filled by the node, and an unbounded map there is remote-controlled memory growth against the 10 §9.4 budget. **Found only because the test double is a *provider* at the wire rather than an adapter written to the transport's own interface**; a double built to match the interface would have called the methods in the order the implementation expected. |
| V-84 | **The read interface let the *transport* choose the block a value was labelled with** | 10 §2.1, §4.2; INV-FE-2 | found + fixed 2026-08-03 (F3) | `storage(key, type)` took no block: the transport read at whatever it considered current, and `FinalizedReader` labelled the result with the pin it was holding. The `#assertStillPinned()` guard looked like it prevented this and did not — it ran **before** the read, so a head that advanced in between produced a value read at N+1 carrying a `verified-finalized` status for N. Nothing about the value can detect that; it is individually valid and its provenance is a lie, which is the precise thing `Finalized<T>` exists to make impossible. Fixed by passing the block explicitly (`storage(at, …)` / `call(at, …)`), so "read at the block I pinned" is unbypassable rather than checked around, and the transport fails rather than substituting. The regression test asserts **on the wire**, because the returned value cannot distinguish the two. Note the converse was also wrong to want: a reader that died whenever the head moved would have a useful life of one block time — pinning exists so it does not. |
| V-83 | **The `ChainHeadTransport` interface shipped synchronous and cannot be implemented** | 10 §4.1, §4.2; INV-FE-1 | found + fixed 2026-08-03 while writing the smoldot transport (F3) | The read layer landed with `pinnedBlock()`/`storage()`/`call()` returning values rather than promises, and its suite passed. smoldot runs in a **Web Worker** (10 §4.1) and every answer arrives by `postMessage`, so the only synchronous implementation is a main-thread block on `Atomics.wait` — which needs cross-origin isolation the Arweave distribution does not control (12 §5.1), and which freezes the UI for the duration of a proof-backed read. The interface was therefore satisfiable by a **test double and by nothing else**: exactly the failure where a mock agrees with a contract no real implementation can meet, and the suite reports the agreement. Fixed by making the interface async and driving the suite through the real `ChainHeadConnection` rather than a bespoke adapter. |
| V-72 | pnpm reproducibility for the 12 §1.1 build recipe — does pnpm's content-addressed store leak absolute paths into sourcemaps? | 12 §1.1; 15 §4.8 | complete (2026-08-03) | **PASS.** Two Vite 8 / pnpm 10.23 builds at different absolute path depths with **separate stores** produced a byte-identical tree (`c5360712cc2505fe…`) and **zero** absolute paths in `dist/`. pnpm's virtual store lives inside the project at `node_modules/.pnpm`, so emitted sources are relative. **Caveat that became a recipe pin:** those relative paths encode the store layout (`../../node_modules/.pnpm/<pkg>@<ver>/…`), so a hoisted install yields identical app bytes and a *different* sourcemap — `node-linker` is therefore part of the pinned recipe, not left to default. 12 §1.1 amended `npm ci` → `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` on this evidence |
| V-73 | Polkadot Product SDK — does `@parity/product-sdk` exist, and can it carry Bleavit? (the user-required architectural proof, six questions) | 10 §4; 15 §2 | desk research complete (2026-08-03); PROD-1…6 open | **It exists** — `@parity/product-sdk@0.20.0`, Apache-2.0, Parity-published, `polkadot-api ^2.1.6`; the signing codec carries raw `method` bytes, `signedExtensions`, `metadataHash`/`mode` (RFC-0078) and `assetId`, so every Bleavit extrinsic fits and custom descriptors are unconstrained. **CORRECTED 2026-08-03:** the first reading of this — *"the host is a WebSocket RPC proxy, not a light client"*, inferred from zero `smoldot` hits in the SDK source — **was wrong**. The connection layer supports **both** (*"one underlying WebSocket (or light client) per chain"*) and ships a full smoldot recipe; the zero-hit result meant the wiring is a recipe for the host implementer, not that the capability is absent. The conclusion survives on a sharper fact: smoldot there needs a chain spec, `polkadot-api` ships built-in specs for **relay chains only**, and the README states outright that **"parachains fall back to WebSocket"** — any other genesis hash throws *Light client for chain X is not supported*. That is the same fact as "chain specs are not accepted" seen from the other side. So a host-routed **Bleavit** connection is WebSocket-backed ⇒ `provider` forever under 10 §2.2 ⇒ **a host-routed Product build cannot sign in normal mode** — not for want of light-client capability, but because there is no channel to supply the spec it would need. Whether the *deployed* devnet host enables even the relay light-client path is **not publicly determinable** (the docs say only that a config service distributes "RPC endpoints") — that is PROD-2. Chain support is operator-configured and runtime-detectable; chain specs are not accepted. Report: `app/docs/product-sdk-compatibility.md`. Conclusion: Product stays an **optional** target; the standalone adapters are canonical |

## Decision log

Spec changes and other project decisions (rule R-1, AGENTS.md).

| Date | Amendment | Authorized by | Docs touched |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-04 | **Doc 10 edits (R-1) from the round-3 review; no 02 change, so no contract bump.** (1) **§10.1 gains `app/packages/handoff-envelope`** and the edge rules gain two clauses. The package carries the §13.1 envelope conventions — canonical JSON and the digest pre-image — which all three formats share and which must therefore have exactly one implementation: two copies are two answers to the one question that must have exactly one, *which bytes are hashed*. It is a **separate package rather than a module in `contexts`** for a firewall reason, and that is the part worth recording: `contexts` is the outbound half and depends on `chain-client` for `Finalized<T>`, so a shared module living there would give the **inbound** parser a transitive path to a chain connection — against §13's second load-bearing sentence, that the inbound format carries no chain state. The second clause states plainly that **no package on a handoff path imports anything external**, node built-ins included: the previous rule was a denylist of network libraries, and a denylist only forbids what somebody thought of (`import ky` defeated it while every gate stayed green). (2) **§13.3's `FE-HANDOFF-004` class widens** from "foreign field inside `action`/`limits`" to "a closed core object (`binding`, `action`, `limits`)". This corrects the text to match §13.1's own rule rather than changing a decision: §13.1 tolerates extras "at the top level **only**", which already closes every nested core object, and `binding` is the one object whose entire job is to pin which chain a document is for. | 2026-08-03 | **Hosted-question slots are sold at a demand-responsive descending price, not first-come-first-served (N14), and the slot cap becomes a graduated latch rather than a governance promise (N15).** User ruling, reached across three exchanges that each corrected the previous design, so the reasoning is recorded rather than just the outcome. **(1) The gap.** Today's admission is `LiveQuestionCount < max_live` — pure first-come-first-served at a posted two-part tariff. Under contention that allocates by transaction latency, not by value: sixteen mediocre questions can lock out an important one, and a freed slot is a bot race. 16 §736 already reasons about scarcity (*"pricing scarce capacity at marginal cost prices it at zero"*) but prices it only with a floor, which is scarcity-aware pricing without a scarcity-aware **allocator**. **(2) Why not Polkadot's coretime auction, which the user proposed.** Its descending price transfers; the rest does not. Coretime sells homogeneous cores on one synchronized 28-day clock, and hosted questions have client-chosen windows that free asynchronously, so there is no batch of identical units to auction. Its renewal right protects a parachain whose core loss is existential, whereas a question simply ends — and a renewal right here would let a client squat the service. Most importantly, **its price controller exists to drive utilization toward a target**, which is correct where selling more cores does not degrade the cores; N12 measured that selling more hosted slots *does* degrade Bleavit's own governance, so importing a quantity-discovering controller would point the feedback loop backwards and make scarcity profitable — the precise pressure TH-73 names. Adopted: adaptive price, hard governance-set quantity. **(3) The user then found the real hole in my first mechanism.** Occupancy pricing is a state function with no memory of velocity, so it cannot answer *"will the price rise if slots get acquired too quickly?"* — sixteen slots taken in one block price identically to sixteen taken over three weeks. A jump-on-purchase term alone does **not** fix it either: after a quiet period the term has decayed, so the first snipe of a freed slot is still cheap. What fixes it is an **asymmetry** — the price moves up instantly on purchase and down only gradually toward the floor, **including after a release**, so a freed slot descends from the pre-release level instead of dropping to the new one. That single rule is simultaneously the per-slot Dutch auction, the velocity term and the demand-discovery loop, and it **prices** sniping rather than preventing it (a bot valuing the slot above the premium still wins, which is the mechanism working). **There is deliberately no start-price parameter**: each descent begins from the running price, which is the accumulated record of prior demand — more responsive than coretime's once-per-period controller, and one stored value plus a lazy decay rather than a broker pallet. **(4) Derivation anchor, and the caveat that constrains it (R-2 step 2).** The N12 competing-venue curve measures decision-grade formation loss per unit of external occupancy, so the marginal slot can be priced at its marginal **measured** damage, valued through the existing `sec.prize.*` keys — a price that is a function of harm rather than a number someone liked, rising steeply exactly where the measurement says damage accelerates. But mapping slots to a diversion fraction runs through the proportional-to-depth flow model that 16 §8.4 now records as **anchored, not derived, with an unsafe error direction**, so the curve MUST be derived from the **0.75 stress rung, not the 0.50 arming rung**: over-pricing costs revenue, under-pricing costs decisions, and the hard cap bounds the unsafe direction regardless, which is what makes this shippable at all. **(5) Two gaming findings that change N15's shape**, both surfaced by carrying the sniping lens into the latch. A **binary** latch creates its own race — operators watching contest capital approach the threshold will register before the cliff — so the response must be graduated, with no cliff to race. And a latch that **grandfathers incumbents pays them to cause it**: locking out new entrants while live questions continue makes a slot-holder's position more valuable precisely when Bleavit is damaged, so suppressing Bleavit's own contest capital becomes profitable for an incumbent. Answered by raising the price for everyone rather than closing the door, with the increase routed to POL, so the incumbent windfall is taxed into the repair. N15 therefore becomes N14's curve with a second input rather than separate machinery. *(N15 riding N14's curve means it inherits N14's destination, which implementation moved to `MAIN` — see (6).)* **(6) Preserved invariants:** `svc.max_live` remains a hard cap the mechanism can never sell past; the floor keeps going to MAIN as cost recovery; the premium routes to POL only at `seal`, since the fee is refunded on VOID. *(That last clause was mine, not the user's ruling, and it did not survive implementation — the whole scaled fee goes to MAIN. See the 16 §8.6 row below and 16 §8.6 itself: a direct POL credit opens a second money path into protocol subsidy custody, and `MAIN` is what funds POL anyway.)* **No spec text amended by this row** — it records the decision and its derivation obligations; the 16, 13, 08, 14 and 15 amendments land with N14 and N15 themselves, and no parameter value is adopted here. | User, 2026-08-03, by explicit ruling (*"I would rather want to set the price dynamically according to the market demand than at fixed prices"*), after proposing the coretime mechanism and then identifying the velocity gap in my occupancy-only design | None yet — PLAN only; 16/13/08/14/15 amendments land with N14 and N15 |

(b) **13 §5's figures move** from `decide` 404,514 B / `settle_cohort(5)` 384,825 B to **745,551 B** / **725,862 B**, and the local drift ceilings from 512 KiB / 768 KiB to **1 MiB** / **1.25 MiB**. That is a measurement replacing a guess: the A13 collator-compensation term was a hand-written 48,000 B / 1.8 ms estimate and benchmarks at 389,037 B / 4.39 ms. The 8x PoV jump is the generator's synthetic per-key envelope (120 payees' `ForeignAssets::Account` keys charged as independent maximum-depth trie paths, ignoring their shared prefix; recorded proof was 17,874 B, ~22x smaller). The estimate is declared anyway because the error directions are asymmetric — over-declaring PoV costs block capacity, under-declaring yields blocks that exceed their proof budget at execution, and a sparse benchmark trie under-represents production path depth, so `pov_mode = Measured` would be optimistic about exactly the wrong thing. | 2026-07-26 | **SQ-490 item (4) — the absence of a regeneration becomes a gated, per-function property, and the hard/advisory split is set by measurement.** 15 §4.5's existing weight bullet says CI "proves executability, not calibration"; that was a statement about a job which ran every benchmark at `--steps 2 --repeat 1` and **discarded the results**, so it could see a benchmark that crashes and never one that disagrees with the committed file. Amended: a per-commit job now re-measures every pallet and diffs the committed artifact **function by function, never by file date** — a header attributes all of a file's functions to one generation event, which is exactly how two hand-appended functions hid inside an otherwise-generated `pallet_attestor.rs`. **The split between hard-gated and advisory dimensions was measured, and the first measurement changed the design.** Storage dimensions are invariant to sampling fidelity — `pallet_attestor` at 2×1 and 50×20 gave byte-identical `proof_size`/`reads`/`writes` for all six functions while ref_time moved −1.2 %…+64.6 % — which is what makes per-commit re-measurement affordable at all. **Two further generalisations of mine were then wrong, and the full sweep is what caught them.** First I made fitted slopes advisory across fidelities, reasoning a 2-point fit need not equal a 50-point one; `pallet_multisig` (11 component terms) agreed on all 46 quantities, so I made every storage figure hard at any fidelity. Running the sweep over all 31 files then produced **42 \`STALE\` lines across 12 pallets, and most were not drift at all**: gating the intercept and slope *separately* reports the generator's own re-decomposition of one measured cost — `pallet_collator_selection::set_candidacy_bond` moves its proof slope 901→1,306 at 2×1 while its worst-case writes stay at exactly 201. So the comparison is now on **worst-case totals** (base + slope × component high), the same quantity `check-weight-regression.py` uses. And the invariance claim does **not** hold universally: re-measuring `pallet_collator_selection`, constant-weight functions agree 2/2 while **component-bearing functions differ 5 of 9**, with `new_session` losing its per-candidate write slope entirely — worst-case writes **100 at 50×20 against 3 at 2×1**. A 2-point fit can miss a linear term, and missing it *understates*, so the rule that survived is: constant-weight totals hard at any fidelity (the class the 8-vs-261-reads defect belonged to, so the cheap per-commit run still catches the real thing), component-bearing totals hard only at matching fidelity and advisory otherwise, ref_time advisory always, and component ranges — declared by the fixture, not fitted — hard always. Full-fidelity coverage of component functions is a release-time obligation that must be reported, not implied. Two obligations added with it: one unsatisfiable fixture MUST NOT discard its pallet's other functions (the state that froze all 39 functions of `pallet_assets.rs` at one date), and a function carried forward unmeasured MUST carry a marker the gate reads and reports, so "measured long ago" is never silently indistinguishable from "measured now". No 02 surface; contract stays at **v15**. | Delegated (R-1, 2026-07-25) | 15 §4.5 |

| 2026-07-26 | **SQ-181 rulings — `U`'s denominator, `F`'s two unsupplied quantities, and the class of failure `Π` counts.** 05 §4.3 gave all three a formula and none of them an observable source; new §4.3.2 fixes each, and every one is anchored to something that already exists rather than to a new tunable. **`U`:** "scheduled slots" read as parachain blocks makes the ratio identically 1, since `epoch.length` is itself denominated in them — so slots are **relay** slots, measured by `PersistedValidationData.relay_parent_number` advancement across the window, and an empty block is one whose extrinsics are all inherents. **`F`:** `target = 1`, derived from the nominal one-block-per-relay-slot cadence. `Λ_max` is **not** derived and ships `[VERIFY]` with `F` fail-closed. No scale repairs an aggregation mismatch. The correction states the division of labour instead: the dead-man owns the tail, `U` owns the count of unfilled slots, `F` owns *sustained* degradation — which is what makes the median right, and also why `Λ_max` has no anchor. Registration is the choice point. Structurally free, because `S` is a `min` carrying no weights (the weight-sum rule binds `C`, `P` and `A`, never `S`), and liveness stays priced by `U` for the count and the dead-man for the tail. `F` keeps id 11 and becomes registrable as a later `MetricSpec` version once Phase-2 evidences `Λ_max`. v1 ships `S = min(U, D_eff)` on two fully-derived signals rather than three with one guess. **`Π`:** an event counts iff the runtime detected a violation of an assumption it holds unconditionally, the fallback discarded correctness-relevant state or engaged a fail-static latch, **and** no defined path restores what was lost. It is redundant against a control that already exists: `execute_coretime_renewal` debits `ops.coretime`, and refilling that line needs the `FutarchyTreasury` origin, so a sustained escalation *already* surfaces as a governance-visible refill request. And it would invert the correct risk ordering — the one failure this call may not risk is `SoldOut`, so any mechanism that can refuse a renewal on price grounds is more dangerous than the escalation it prevents. The rule is therefore stated in 09 §4 as an operating margin ("as late as the observed remaining-core margin allows, never later") with the procedure in RB-TREASURY, and the call stays timing-agnostic. **What this costs: the policy is unenforced and can be forgotten.** Accepted knowingly — the failure mode is a slow, fully reversible price ratchet whose signature is visible (rising refill cadence with flat `end_price`), and one late renewal repairs it entirely. | Me, under R-1 (the user owns both sides of the 02 §13 sign-off and has delegated it, 2026-07-25); no 02 surface is touched, so no contract bump | `08-treasury-and-economics.md` §10.1, `09-execution-upgrades-and-rollout.md` §4, `deploy/runbooks/RB-TREASURY.md` |
| 2026-07-31 | **SQ-540(b) ruled: the reserve haircut has THREE maintenance carve-outs, and proposer rewards are not a fourth — they are not a carve-out at all.** The sweep reported 08 §1.2 enumerating two carve-outs against four code paths and framed it as a scope-A solvency divergence to be closed "either way". Both halves of that framing were wrong. **Collator compensation is a genuine third carve-out** and the argument is D-9's own, applied beneath itself: coretime keeps the chain's core, collator pay keeps someone willing to author on it, and without blocks the reserve probe never runs and the flag never clears — so gating it would make the freeze self-sealing. It is bounded to the dedicated `COLLATOR` pot, pays for work already performed, and `fund_budget_line` stays ungated under the flag because gating *that* would defeat carve-out (a). **Proposer rewards are a crystallized obligation**, in the class §1.2 already exempts as "existing stream claims". The check that decided it is the one that caught two P1s on the collator work: fail-soft protects against an unbacked claim, not against non-payment. `mark_executed` calls `do_proposer_reward` once and discards the result by design, so a haircut gate would **destroy** the reward rather than defer it — permanent forfeiture over a condition the proposer neither caused nor can influence, which G-1 and R-7 both forbid. Amending the code to "enforce the spec" would have been the unsafe direction here, and the spec was simply incomplete. | Me, under R-1; audit scope A, so the ruling is pinned by a regression test rather than left as prose | `08-treasury-and-economics.md` §1.2, `crates/futarchy-treasury-core/src/lib.rs` (test) |
| 2026-07-31 | **SQ-540(e) implemented: the XCM execution fee is retained as treasury revenue, and DOT deliberately is not recognized.** Two decisions. **(1) Capture, not discard.** The chain already prices every inbound message at the governed 09 §6.1 rates; dropping the payment was unfinished wiring, not a policy. Worth stating precisely what dropping meant, because "burning revenue" overstates it: local USDC is backed by the sovereign reserve, so a burned fee left the reserve over-backing issuance — real protocol value, but off-ledger, invisible to `nav()`, and reachable only by a governance reconciliation. Routing it to `MAIN` leaves issuance and the reserve in the same relation and makes the value spendable. **(2) USDC is recognized as NAV; DOT is deposited but not.** 08 §1.2 marks DOT at 0 in NAV, so crediting DOT to `MAIN` would inflate NAV by exactly the term the treasury refuses to count — custody is still taken, since the asset is real, but recognition is USDC-only. The ordering is also load-bearing and is asserted: recognition follows a successful deposit and never precedes it, so this path cannot make the internal ledger claim more than the pot holds (I-33), while a deposit *without* recognition would be equally wrong in the other direction — NAV reads the internal ledger, so the revenue would exist and be unusable. | Me, under R-1; audit scope A, so both halves and the failure path are pinned by tests rather than left as prose. | 2026-07-21 | tooling — CI parity checker | **`tools/ci/check-ci-parity.py`** — the direct remediation of the Codex finding on PR #125. Adding `check-weight-regression.py` to `rust-workspace-gates.sh` broke the Rust CI job: the checker defaults its base to `git merge-base HEAD origin/main`, the dedicated `Weight regression` job resolves it only because it sets `fetch-depth: 0`, and the Rust job's bare `actions/checkout@v7` fetches just the triggering commit. Every local gate run stayed green because the worktree had `origin/main` fetched — **running the same script locally is structurally blind to this class of failure**. The checker runs each environment-sensitive gate in the working tree and again in a shallow single-branch clone shaped like `actions/checkout@v7`, and fails on any that diverge. The line is 79 characters, well inside `max_width`, which is why it *reads* as correctly formatted. **Correction to this row's first version, which blamed a nightly-vs-stable difference: it is not one.** `main`'s `Rust workspace` job runs **stable** `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and fails on the identical line, so both toolchains want the split and the fuzz workspace merely surfaced it first. The real cause is duller and more useful to record: **the pin test was added after the last `cargo fmt` run and formatting was never re-checked** — the `--changed` scope and the targeted test runs that followed do not re-run fmt. **It merged, and `main` has been red since**: `tests.rs:5541`, failing both `Rust workspace` and `Fuzzing`. The fix rides in on this PR because #219 is the only branch open. Verified both directions before pushing: nightly reformats it and then stable's check exits 0 on the result, so the two toolchains agree on the split form and this cannot ping-pong. **The instructive part is not the formatting, it is the blind spot's shape** — `fuzz/` is a separate cargo workspace with its own lockfile and toolchain precisely so libFuzzer and nightly cannot perturb the runtime workspace's `=`-exact stable2606 pins, and the price of that isolation is that the main workspace's gates cannot see it. Three earlier failures this session came from the same seam (a stale `ReportDraft` construction, a stale `Cargo.lock`, and a prior fmt difference), and the N10 brief already warns about it by name. Running `cargo fmt --all` from `fuzz/` is cheap and should follow any edit to a crate the fuzz targets reach, which — because fmt follows path dependencies rather than workspace members — includes the runtime. | Rerun the fuzz gate on the pushed head; keep a standing CI watcher rather than reporting green off a partial rollup |

| 2026-08-02 | Two adversarial review rounds on the partition, and what each caught that gates could not | **Every gate was green when the partition first reported done — 439 runtime tests, 10⁶ property cases, limit coverage, weight regression, docs — and it still carried four defects, so the plan's Risk 1 ("needs an independent adversarial review before merge, not just green gates") paid for itself twice.** Round 1 found: `H` moving with **zero** registered clients (the feature reproducing its own failure mode from another direction); genuine `Operational` dispatches unable to reach the Operational reserve; a test named PT-10 that was not PT-10; and 05/16 contradicting each other. Round 2, on the repairs, found the fixes were only *partial*: the continuous algebra cancelled but the **integer** arithmetic did not — double-ceiling on scale and target put `H` one unit **high** at some inputs, and high is the unsafe direction because it reports the chain healthier than it is. **Both rounds beat my own analysis on a specific point, which is the argument for the practice rather than against it.** On the Operational question I asked "can clients starve operational calls?", proved the counters disjoint, and stopped; the real defect was the inverse — operational work could no longer reach its own reserve.
